Important new evidence•Formal CTAD 2026 conference report and sponsor numerical tables•November 17, 2026

CELIA two-year extension strengthens the diranersen signal but remains nonconfirmatory

At week 96, the 60 mg twice-yearly group had a sponsor-reported 1.09-point CDR-SB advantage versus participants originally assigned placebo, but the comparison extends beyond the randomized placebo-controlled period and follows a failed prespecified dose-response endpoint.

Key quantitative results: At week 96, 60 mg twice yearly (n=60) versus the original placebo group (n=115) showed a reported 1.09-point CDR-SB difference, described as 38% less decline; confidence intervals and multiplicity-adjusted p values were not supplied.

Clinical TrialsCSFTotal tauTau PETDisease-modifying treatment

Added November 25, 2026 · NCT05399888

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

CELIA's updated extension analysis shows wider numerical separation at two years for twice-yearly 60 mg diranersen. The signal is clinically interesting and supports phase 3 development, but it is not confirmatory: the original dose-response endpoint failed, only 60 participants remained in the highlighted dose group, and the week-96 comparator had begun transitioning to active treatment.

Study design

CELIA randomized 416 anti-amyloid-naive participants with MCI due to AD or mild AD dementia to intrathecal diranersen or placebo for 18 months. The two-year analysis compared 60 participants who remained on 60 mg twice yearly with 115 participants originally assigned placebo; by week 96 the latter had received either no diranersen or one dose after entering the open-label extension.

Key quantitative results

  • At week 96, 60 mg twice yearly (n=60) versus the original placebo group (n=115) showed a reported 1.09-point CDR-SB difference, described as 38% less decline; confidence intervals and multiplicity-adjusted p values were not supplied.
  • Sponsor tables reported week-96 slowing of 54% on ADAS-Cog13, 38% on MMSE, 30% on ADCS-ADL-MCI, 38% on ADCOMS, and 46% on modified iADRS.
  • At 18 months, the 60 mg subgroup had shown a 0.54-point CDR-SB difference (26% slowing), while the prespecified primary dose-response analysis was negative.
  • The 18-month placebo-controlled biomarker report described broad reductions in tau PET, CSF p-tau181, and plasma p-tau217, but did not establish that those changes mediated clinical benefit.
  • Diranersen was reported as generally well tolerated through two years with no new safety signal; detailed event rates were not provided in the public conference summary.

What changed

The CTAD extension report adds 96-week clinical comparisons and shows increasing numerical separation, while leaving the original negative primary analysis and nonrandomized extension limitations intact.

Strength of evidence

Moderate signal-generating evidence from a randomized phase 2 program followed by an open-label extension. Certainty is limited by the failed prespecified dose-response endpoint, the highlighted 60-participant subgroup, crossover exposure in the comparator, absent confidence intervals, and sponsor-only conference reporting.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings justify phase 3 confirmation but do not support clinical use or prove that biomarker lowering translates into benefit.

Field medical relevance

Separates a promising longer-term tau-lowering signal from confirmatory efficacy and preserves the distinction between biomarker response and clinical utility.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Tau biomarker reduction supports target engagement but does not establish assay utility, mediation, or clinical efficacy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No approval, routine availability, coverage, or reimbursement change. A phase 3 program is still needed.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the study positive on its primary endpoint?
No. Dose response on CDR-SB was not demonstrated.
Is the week-96 comparison still fully randomized and placebo controlled?
No. It comes from the open-label extension; the original placebo group had received either no active dose or one active dose by week 96.
Do the tau biomarker changes prove clinical benefit?
No. They support target engagement, but mediation of clinical benefit was not established.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Failed prespecified dose-response primary endpoint
  • Open-label extension with crossover exposure in the original placebo group
  • Highlighted 60 mg group included 60 participants
  • Confidence intervals and adjusted p values were not reported publicly
  • Sponsor conference report without peer-reviewed full results

Correction notes

  • November 25, 2026: Updated the stable CELIA brief with the November 17 CTAD two-year extension report. The new 96-week comparison is not randomized through the full interval and does not reverse the failed prespecified dose-response endpoint.

Primary source · May primary-endpoint disclosure · July 18-month numerical results · Trial registry

Biogen. Diranersen demonstrates increasing clinical benefit at two years in early Alzheimer's disease. CTAD 2026 conference report. November 17, 2026. NCT05399888. Sponsor-reported results.

Important new evidence•Formal CTAD 2026 phase 3 presentation with sponsor numerical tables•November 16, 2026

POLARIS-AD is positive only in the prespecified monotherapy population

AR1001 missed the 52-week CDR-SB comparison in all 1,535 participants but met the multiplicity-controlled objective in the 604-person subgroup not using symptomatic AD drugs, with a 0.44-point difference.

Key quantitative results: In the overall population, the week-52 CDR-SB difference was -0.11 points versus placebo (p=0.4015), which was not significant.

Clinical TrialsCSFCSF cGMPCSF p-tau217Disease-modifying treatment

Added November 25, 2026 · NCT05531526; CTAD 2026 POLARIS-AD

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

POLARIS-AD produced a statistically valid but narrow phase 3 result: the prespecified monotherapy population met the multiplicity-controlled CDR-SB objective, while the overall population did not. Secondary cognitive findings were nominal, biomarker changes were mixed, and discontinuations were more frequent with AR1001. Full peer-reviewed results and regulatory review are needed before interpreting the subgroup as an indication.

Study design

POLARIS-AD randomized 1,535 participants with early AD at approximately 230 sites in 13 countries to oral AR1001 30 mg daily or placebo for 52 weeks. CDR-SB was tested in two prespecified primary populations: all participants and 604 participants not using an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor or memantine at baseline. Success required significance in at least one population under the prespecified multiplicity procedure.

Key quantitative results

  • In the overall population, the week-52 CDR-SB difference was -0.11 points versus placebo (p=0.4015), which was not significant.
  • In the prespecified monotherapy population (n=604), the CDR-SB difference was -0.44 points (p=0.0266), reported as 31% less decline and meeting the multiplicity-controlled primary objective.
  • Monotherapy-population secondary results included ADAS-Cog13 -1.16 points (p=0.0798) and MMSE +0.7 points (p=0.0232); these were reported as nominal rather than confirmatory.
  • CSF p-tau217 differences were -3.52 pg/mL overall (p=0.1784) and -5.34 pg/mL in monotherapy (p=0.0402); CSF Aβ42/40 did not differ. CSF cGMP increased with AR1001.
  • Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 69.0% with AR1001 and 66.4% with placebo; serious events were 10.0% and 9.8%, fatal events 0.5% and 0.3%, and study-drug discontinuation 5.2% and 1.7%, respectively.

What changed

The first phase 3 readout establishes a mixed outcome: no overall-population benefit, but a prespecified monotherapy population met the statistical primary objective.

Strength of evidence

High for the randomized phase 3 overall and prespecified-population estimates, but limited by sponsor-only topline reporting, a modest absolute effect, failure in the overall population, and lack of peer-reviewed full methods and subgroup characterization.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The results support regulatory discussion and further analysis but do not justify clinical use. The monotherapy finding should not be generalized to patients receiving symptomatic AD drugs or to the full early-AD population.

Field medical relevance

Important for oral disease-modifying-therapy development and for interpreting phase 3 programs with dual prespecified populations and mixed clinical and biomarker findings.

Quanterix or platform relevance

CSF biomarkers were secondary target-engagement outcomes. The central question was clinical treatment efficacy, so the report is not classified as Biomarkers.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No immediate access change. Regulatory discussions are planned, but approval and coverage have not occurred.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was POLARIS-AD positive in the overall population?
No. The overall CDR-SB difference was -0.11 points with p=0.4015.
Was the monotherapy analysis post hoc?
No. It was a prespecified primary population within the multiplicity procedure, but its applicability remains limited to participants not taking symptomatic AD drugs at baseline.
Is AR1001 available for clinical use?
No. It remains investigational and has not been authorized for Alzheimer disease.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Sponsor-reported conference topline without peer-reviewed full results
  • Overall population did not meet the primary endpoint
  • Monotherapy effect was modest and population-specific
  • Secondary and biomarker results were nominal
  • Higher treatment discontinuation with AR1001

Primary source · Trial registry

Sha SJ, et al. POLARIS-AD phase 3 topline efficacy and safety results. Presented at CTAD 2026; November 16, 2026. NCT05531526. Sponsor numerical report.

Important new evidence•Formal CTAD 2026 pivotal-trial presentation with sponsor numerical report•November 16, 2026

HOPE misses its overall endpoint despite a favorable mild-AD subgroup

The 673-person pivotal trial did not meet its overall primary endpoint; in a prespecified 395-person mild-AD subgroup, the sponsor reported 56% less ADCS-ADL decline and 47% less CDR-SB decline, both nominal findings without published absolute differences.

Key quantitative results: The trial did not meet its primary endpoint in the overall 673-participant population.

Clinical TrialsNonpharmacologic treatment

Added November 25, 2026 · NCT05637801; CTAD 2026 HOPE

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

HOPE's overall primary endpoint was negative, so the favorable prespecified mild-AD subgroup cannot establish efficacy by itself. The subgroup effects are clinically interesting but were reported only as relative slowing with nominal p values and without absolute changes or confidence intervals. Full peer-reviewed results and regulatory assessment are needed before the device can be considered clinically effective.

Study design

HOPE randomized 673 people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease to daily Spectris 40 Hz light-and-sound stimulation or a sham device for 12 months. The pivotal study evaluated functional and global clinical outcomes and included a prespecified mild-AD subgroup of 395 participants.

Key quantitative results

  • The trial did not meet its primary endpoint in the overall 673-participant population.
  • In the prespecified mild-AD subgroup (n=395), the sponsor reported 56% less decline on ADCS-ADL (nominal p=0.016) and 47% less decline on CDR-SB (nominal p=0.004) at 12 months.
  • Absolute between-group point differences, confidence intervals, and the full multiplicity framework for the subgroup results were not publicly reported.
  • An exploratory What Matters Most outcome was reported as 60% less decline (nominal p=0.04).
  • The sponsor reported no unanticipated adverse device effects but did not provide a complete event-rate table in the public release.

What changed

The first pivotal HOPE readout establishes a negative overall result alongside favorable prespecified mild-AD subgroup findings that may support further regulatory review but remain nonconfirmatory.

Strength of evidence

Moderate for the negative overall pivotal result and low-to-moderate for subgroup efficacy because the mild-AD analysis was prespecified but reported only through sponsor conference materials, with nominal p values and incomplete absolute and safety data.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Spectris should not be used as an established Alzheimer treatment outside research or an authorized access pathway. The subgroup result warrants full review and replication but does not override failure of the overall primary endpoint.

Field medical relevance

Provides a pivotal test of sensory gamma stimulation and illustrates why subgroup-relative effects must be separated from a trial's overall primary result and from regulatory authorization.

Quanterix or platform relevance

This report evaluates a therapeutic 40 Hz light-and-sound device, not a biomarker measurement platform.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No current clinical access or coverage change. Breakthrough Device designation and a planned De Novo discussion do not authorize the device.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did HOPE meet its overall primary endpoint?
No. The overall 673-participant pivotal population did not meet the primary endpoint.
Were the mild-AD subgroup findings prespecified?
Yes, but the public report provides nominal relative effects without absolute differences, confidence intervals, or full multiplicity details.
Is Spectris FDA authorized for Alzheimer disease?
No. Breakthrough Device designation facilitates development and review; it is not marketing authorization.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Overall primary endpoint was not met
  • Sponsor-reported conference topline without peer-reviewed full results
  • Subgroup effects reported as relative slowing without absolute differences or confidence intervals
  • Nominal p values and incomplete multiplicity information
  • Limited publicly reported adverse-event detail

Primary source · Trial registry

Sabbagh MN, et al. HOPE pivotal trial of Spectris 40 Hz light-and-sound stimulation. Presented at CTAD 2026; November 16, 2026. NCT05637801. Sponsor numerical report.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed randomized phase 2 trial, verified after the November 23 catch-up review•November 10, 2026

Bepranemab misses the phase 2 CDR-SB endpoint

In 460 treated participants, neither bepranemab dose improved week-80 CDR-SB versus placebo; the 90 mg/kg arm numerically declined more, while safety was broadly similar across groups.

Key quantitative results: Least-squares mean CDR-SB change was 2.15 with 90 mg/kg, 1.85 with 45 mg/kg, and 1.81 with placebo.

Clinical TrialsTau PETTau PETDisease-modifying treatment

Added November 25, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/S1474-4422(26)00357-1; PMID:43008775; NCT04867616

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

A mid-region tau antibody did not slow clinical decline in the overall phase 2 population. Exploratory tau-PET and cognitive signals remain hypothesis-generating and cannot outweigh the negative primary endpoint. The neutral result narrows current tau-antibody development questions toward baseline tau burden, APOE stratification, and biomarker-powered designs.

Study design

The trial randomized 466 adults aged 50–80 with prodromal-to-mild AD at 85 sites to intravenous bepranemab 45 mg/kg, 90 mg/kg, or placebo every four weeks for 76 weeks. The full analysis set included 460 participants, and the primary endpoint was week-80 change in CDR-SB.

Key quantitative results

  • Least-squares mean CDR-SB change was 2.15 with 90 mg/kg, 1.85 with 45 mg/kg, and 1.81 with placebo.
  • The 90 mg/kg difference versus placebo was 0.34 points (95% CI -0.09 to 0.78; p=0.12), and the 45 mg/kg difference was 0.04 points (95% CI -0.40 to 0.47; p=0.87). Neither favored bepranemab significantly.
  • Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 91% of each bepranemab group and 90% of placebo; no treatment-related neuroinflammatory clinical or MRI signal was identified.
  • Adverse events leading to death occurred in 4 participants (1%) across both bepranemab groups and 6 participants (4%) with placebo; none were judged treatment related.
  • Tau-PET and ADAS-Cog14 differences were exploratory and require prospective confirmation in trials powered for those outcomes.

What changed

Peer-reviewed results now confirm that bepranemab did not meet its primary clinical endpoint despite an acceptable safety profile and exploratory biomarker signals.

Strength of evidence

Strong evidence for failure of the prespecified CDR-SB endpoint from a multicenter randomized, double-blind trial. Evidence for tau-PET or subgroup benefit is low because those findings were exploratory and not the powered primary analysis.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Bepranemab should not be used outside research. The report does not establish clinical efficacy for a mid-region tau antibody.

Field medical relevance

Clarifies the current limits of tau-antibody development and prevents exploratory tau-PET signals from being interpreted as treatment benefit.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Tau PET was an exploratory outcome; the trial's central question was treatment efficacy, so this is not classified as a Biomarkers report.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No access pathway changes; bepranemab remains investigational.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did either bepranemab dose slow CDR-SB decline?
No. Neither dose differed significantly from placebo, and the 90 mg/kg point estimate numerically favored placebo.
Was there a new MRI inflammatory safety signal?
No treatment-related neuroinflammatory clinical or MRI signal was identified.
Do the exploratory tau-PET findings establish efficacy?
No. They are hypothesis-generating and need a prospectively powered trial.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Phase 2 trial not powered to confirm exploratory tau-PET effects
  • No imputation for missing data
  • Subgroup and biomarker findings are hypothesis-generating
  • Sponsor-funded trial

Primary source · DOI

Barton ME, Byrnes W, van den Steen B, et al. Safety, tolerability, and efficacy of bepranemab in people living with prodromal-to-mild Alzheimer's disease: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet Neurol. Published online November 10, 2026. doi:10.1016/S1474-4422(26)00357-1.

Amyloid PET reference region changed estimates of treatment response

Reference-region choice affected apparent longitudinal amyloid change; a favorable exploratory association for white matter did not survive the same-tracer sensitivity analysis.

Key quantitative results: Cerebellar gray matter and whole cerebellum showed burden-dependent bias versus eroded white matter (quadratic p=0.021 and p=0.013, respectively).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidCentiloidQuantification

Added November 23, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13195-026-02256-5

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Reference-region choice affected apparent longitudinal amyloid change; a favorable exploratory association for white matter did not survive the same-tracer sensitivity analysis. Read apparent change in the context of tracer, reference region and validated pipeline; avoid a universal switch based on this study.

Study design

Analysis of serial amyloid PET in 138 participants receiving amyloid-targeted treatment; compared cerebellar and white-matter reference regions.

Key quantitative results

  • Cerebellar gray matter and whole cerebellum showed burden-dependent bias versus eroded white matter (quadratic p=0.021 and p=0.013, respectively).
  • The eroded-white-matter change association with cognition (p=0.029) was not confirmed in the same-tracer subset.

What changed

Cerebellar gray matter and whole cerebellum showed burden-dependent bias versus eroded white matter (quadratic p=0.021 and p=0.013, respectively).

Strength of evidence

Longitudinal PET analysis in a treated clinical cohort. Key constraints: observational analysis.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Read apparent change in the context of tracer, reference region and validated pipeline; avoid a universal switch based on this study.

Field medical relevance

Interpret alongside these constraints: Tracer effects and reference-region comparability; Exploratory association not robust to a restriction.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Read apparent change in the context of tracer, reference region and validated pipeline; avoid a universal switch based on this study.

Access or reimbursement relevance

These results do not by themselves establish routine availability or payer coverage.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does this establish eroded white matter as the new standard?
No. The comparison flags measurement bias; the clinical association was not robust in a sensitivity analysis.

  • Tracer effects and reference-region comparability
  • Exploratory association not robust to a restriction

Late acquisition dynamics differed across two amyloid PET tracers

Late tracer kinetics differed, particularly in white matter; small average bias in abbreviated reconstructions does not establish clinical interchangeability.

Key quantitative results: White-matter slope difference was 0.00628 ratio/min (95% CI, 0.00529–0.00727); cortical difference was 0.00191 (0.00069–0.00314).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloidSUVRAcquisition

Added November 23, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s11307-026-02157-x

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Late tracer kinetics differed, particularly in white matter; small average bias in abbreviated reconstructions does not establish clinical interchangeability. Keep tracer, timing and reconstruction consistent when interpreting serial or cross-site quantitative data.

Study design

Retrospective comparison in 117 clinical scans of late temporal dynamics and shortened reconstructions for florbetaben versus flutemetamol.

Key quantitative results

  • White-matter slope difference was 0.00628 ratio/min (95% CI, 0.00529–0.00727); cortical difference was 0.00191 (0.00069–0.00314).
  • The cortical estimate attenuated in the same-scanner analysis. The first 15 minutes showed small average bias against the full 20-minute reconstruction.

What changed

White-matter slope difference was 0.00628 ratio/min (95% CI, 0.00529–0.00727); cortical difference was 0.00191 (0.00069–0.00314).

Strength of evidence

Retrospective acquisition-method comparison. Key constraints: retrospective comparison.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Keep tracer, timing and reconstruction consistent when interpreting serial or cross-site quantitative data.

Field medical relevance

Interpret alongside these constraints: Potential scanner and protocol confounding; No prospective equivalence validation for shortened reads.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Keep tracer, timing and reconstruction consistent when interpreting serial or cross-site quantitative data.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No. Prospective validation of the shortened workflow and its effect on individual reads is still needed.

Elecsys p-tau217 cutoffs performed similarly to locally derived cutoffs in China

Existing Elecsys cutoffs performed similarly to locally derived values in this PET-referenced Chinese cohort, with about one in six in the gray zone.

Key quantitative results: With fixed cutoffs of 0.223 and 0.378 pg/mL, PPA was 96.0% (95% CI 92.3%–98.3%), NPA 92.3% (87.9%–95.4%), and 17.3% were intermediate.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Assay comparison

Added November 23, 2026 · ctad-2026-zuo-elecsys-ptau217-china

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Existing Elecsys cutoffs performed similarly to locally derived values in this PET-referenced Chinese cohort, with about one in six in the gray zone. Use this evidence to prioritize local validation and a reflex plan, not to assume population transportability.

Study design

PET-referenced analysis of 347 participants for derivation and 508 for validation. In the validation cohort, PET positivity was 43.9%.

Key quantitative results

  • With fixed cutoffs of 0.223 and 0.378 pg/mL, PPA was 96.0% (95% CI 92.3%–98.3%), NPA 92.3% (87.9%–95.4%), and 17.3% were intermediate.
  • China-derived cutoffs yielded PPA 96.2% and NPA 90.7%.

What changed

With fixed cutoffs of 0.223 and 0.378 pg/mL, PPA was 96.0% (95% CI 92.3%–98.3%), NPA 92.3% (87.9%–95.4%), and 17.3% were intermediate.

Strength of evidence

Conference diagnostic cutoff derivation and validation. Key constraints: sponsor conference poster, not yet full peer-reviewed report.

Lumipulse blood testing matched CSF accuracy among determinate results

Plasma p-tau217 had similar accuracy to CSF when it yielded a determinate result, but the plasma gray zone was larger, particularly for the ratio.

Key quantitative results: Plasma assay AUCs ranged from 0.90 to 0.96.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217p-tau217/Aβ42Biological confirmation

Added November 23, 2026 · DOI:10.1038/s43587-026-01259-z

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Plasma p-tau217 had similar accuracy to CSF when it yielded a determinate result, but the plasma gray zone was larger, particularly for the ratio. Plan a reflex pathway and compare indeterminacy as well as accuracy before substituting blood for CSF.

Study design

Head-to-head comparison in 514 participants, including real-world primary-care and memory-clinic cohorts, applying prespecified two-cutoff approaches to plasma and CSF against amyloid status.

Key quantitative results

  • Plasma assay AUCs ranged from 0.90 to 0.96.
  • Among determinate clinical-cohort results, p-tau217 accuracy was 90%–97% versus 91% for the clinical CSF approach.
  • In memory clinic/primary care, p-tau217 alone left 16.3%/17.3% intermediate; its ratio left 26.4%/21.8%, compared with 12.4%/10.0% for CSF.
  • With respective labeled cutoffs, the plasma ratio's specificity was 89% in the memory clinic versus 62% in primary care. Standalone p-tau217 used European CE-marked cutoffs; the ratio used FDA-cleared cutoffs.

What changed

Plasma assay AUCs ranged from 0.90 to 0.96.

Strength of evidence

Multicohort head-to-head diagnostic study. Key constraints: accuracy conditional on a determinate result.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Plan a reflex pathway and compare indeterminacy as well as accuracy before substituting blood for CSF.

Field medical relevance

Interpret alongside these constraints: Thresholds and results are assay- and population-specific; Not a test of downstream patient outcomes; Reagent lot changes may affect portability of ratio cutoffs.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Plan a reflex pathway and compare indeterminacy as well as accuracy before substituting blood for CSF.

Access or reimbursement relevance

These results do not by themselves establish routine availability or payer coverage.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should every intermediate plasma result be treated as negative?
No. Intermediate results remain unresolved; consider further workup, CSF, or PET as appropriate.

  • Thresholds and results are assay- and population-specific

  • Reagent lot changes may affect portability of ratio cutoffs

Structured digital APOE disclosure was noninferior to clinician telehealth in eSMARTER

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Structured digital APOE disclosure met noninferiority criteria, but the trial did not establish equivalence for routine portal-only p-tau217 delivery. Consider the safeguards, eligibility and workflow in the trial before drawing conclusions about patient-facing disclosure.

Study design

Remote randomized trial (NCT06459583); 651 participants completed APOE disclosure, 435 digitally and 216 by clinician telehealth. Five hundred opted for p-tau217 disclosure.

Key quantitative results

  • Digital APOE disclosure met prespecified noninferiority margins for knowledge, anxiety and distress at 1–7 days.
  • No significant arm differences were seen after optional p-tau217 disclosure; noninferiority of that outcome was not established.

What changed

Digital APOE disclosure met prespecified noninferiority margins for knowledge, anxiety and distress at 1–7 days.

Strength of evidence

Randomized noninferiority clinical trial. Key constraints: internet-enabled, psychologically screened volunteers.

Important new evidence•FDA 510(k) decision summary•October 8, 2025

FDA cleared Elecsys pTau181 Plasma as a primary-care rule-out aid

At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, the single 0.722 pg/mL cutoff produced 92.7% positive agreement, 51.3% negative agreement, 97.9% NPV, and 22.4% PPV in 312 primary-care patients.

Key label details: At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%–97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%–57.2%).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau181Rule-out triage

Added October 20, 2026 · FDA 510(k) K252163

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The clearance is intentionally asymmetric. A negative result is consistent with a negative amyloid PET and may reduce unnecessary imaging, but nearly half of PET-negative participants tested positive. The FDA summary therefore supports rule-out triage, not standalone confirmation, and shows how low prevalence drives high NPV and low PPV.

Study design

FDA reviewed analytical validation and a pivotal clinical study in 312 evaluable primary-care patients aged at least 55 years who presented with cognitive concerns or impairment. The plasma result at a prespecified 0.722 pg/mL cutoff was compared with majority visual amyloid-PET classification; 41/312 participants were PET positive.

Key label details

  • At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%–97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%–57.2%).
  • At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, NPV was 97.9% (139/142; 95% CI, 94.0%–99.3%) and PPV was 22.4% (38/170; 95% CI, 19.5%–25.0%).
  • Three of 41 PET-positive patients tested negative, while 132 of 271 PET-negative patients tested positive.
  • FDA estimated that negative testing could reduce unnecessary amyloid PET by 45.5% (142/312).
  • The measuring range was 0.300–50.00 pg/mL; no high-dose hook effect was observed through 150 pg/mL.

What changed

This historical criteria-repair entry documents a previously unbriefed FDA-cleared automated p-tau181 rule-out assay and its markedly prevalence-dependent predictive values.

Strength of evidence

High regulatory and analytical-validity evidence with public pivotal performance data. Clinical utility is limited to the cleared initial-assessment aid; prospective patient-outcome benefit, specialty-care use, prognosis, and serial monitoring were not established.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A negative result can support ruling out amyloid pathology in primary care, but a positive result cannot confirm amyloid pathology and should trigger further evaluation. The intended population and low-prevalence setting are integral to interpretation.

Field medical relevance

Provides a concrete comparison point for p-tau217 assays and illustrates why intended use, cutoff architecture, prevalence, PPV, NPV, and referral setting must be separated when discussing blood tests.

Quanterix or platform relevance

This is a fully automated electrochemiluminescence assay with an 18-minute run time and a single negative/positive cutoff. Its intended role differs from three-zone p-tau217 workflows: the high NPV supports rule-out in low-prevalence primary care, while the low PPV means positive results need further investigation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA clearance establishes authorization, not universal laboratory availability, payer coverage, reimbursement, or guideline endorsement. Local ordering and payment require separate verification.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can a positive result confirm Alzheimer disease?
No. PPV was 22.4% in the pivotal primary-care cohort, and the FDA labeling says positive results should be investigated further.
Can the assay be used in specialty clinics?
Its cleared intended use is initial assessment, and the summary states it is not recommended for patients already referred to a specialist.
Can it monitor therapy or predict dementia?
No. Those uses were not established in the cleared labeling.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly source-dated development
  • Low amyloid prevalence produced very low PPV
  • Single binary cutoff leaves many false-positive results
  • Intended use is limited to initial assessment outside specialty care
  • No prognostic, treatment-monitoring, or patient-outcome utility claim

Primary source · FDA 510(k) record

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Elecsys Phospho-Tau (181P) Plasma. 510(k) K252163. Decision October 8, 2025.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world imaging study•October 8, 2026

Real-world lecanemab PET monitoring reveals visual-quantitative discordance

In 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients treated for 6–8 months, amyloid burden fell by 29.39±22.31 Centiloids, but visual and quantitative response agreement was poor to fair (κ 0.205–0.253), supporting explicit Centiloid quantification for serial monitoring rather than visual interpretation alone.

Key quantitative results: Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid CentiloidTau PET SUVRTreatment response monitoring

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261493063

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort shows substantial short-term plaque reduction without measurable cognitive or tau-PET change. Only 12 of 38 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids and five were visually negative. The discordance supports quantitative serial assessment when PET is obtained, but this small uncontrolled cohort cannot prove clinical utility or determine when treatment should stop.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively analyzed 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients with Alzheimer disease who received lecanemab for 6–8 months. Paired tests evaluated Centiloid and cognitive change, kappa measured visual-quantitative agreement, and exploratory regression assessed predictors of amyloid reduction.

Key quantitative results

  • Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.
  • Twelve of 38 patients reached less than 24.1 Centiloids, while only five were visually negative.
  • Visual-quantitative agreement was poor to fair: κ=0.205 for positivity and κ=0.253 for treatment efficacy.
  • Baseline Centiloid burden (standardized β=0.594, p<0.001) and number of treatment cycles (β=0.285, p=0.022) independently predicted greater clearance; tau SUVR had a marginal inverse association (β=-0.238, p=0.052). The multivariable model adjusted R² was 0.507.

What changed

This real-world study directly quantifies the gap between visual and Centiloid-based interpretation during short-term lecanemab therapy and proposes a hybrid screening-and-monitoring workflow.

Strength of evidence

Early real-world evidence with paired PET and quantitative effect estimates, but retrospective, uncontrolled and limited to 38 patients. Visual-reading methods, tracer/scanner generalizability and downstream clinical utility require independent validation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

If serial amyloid PET is obtained, visual negativity alone may miss low residual burden and quantitative Centiloid reporting can add interpretive precision. The study does not establish that routine serial PET improves outcomes or should guide dose changes.

Field medical relevance

Addresses recurring MSL questions about visual versus quantitative reads, low-burden discordance, Centiloid thresholds and PET-based response monitoring under anti-amyloid therapy.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The central comparison is visual versus quantitative amyloid-PET interpretation during lecanemab treatment. Poor agreement indicates that visual and Centiloid assessments are not interchangeable near low residual burden; the study did not validate performance across tracers, scanners or independent readers.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization or coverage change. Serial quantitative PET could increase imaging demand and cost; the study did not evaluate reimbursement or access.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does the study establish routine serial PET monitoring?
No. It shows measurement discordance in a small cohort but did not test whether serial PET improves treatment decisions or outcomes.
Can visual negativity and less than 24.1 Centiloids be treated as equivalent?
No. Twelve patients crossed the quantitative threshold while only five were visually negative, and kappa agreement was low.
Did plaque reduction produce short-term cognitive improvement?
No significant MMSE or MoCA change was detected over 6–8 months.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly published item
  • Retrospective single-cohort design
  • Only 38 patients
  • No untreated comparator
  • Short 6–8-month follow-up
  • No validation across tracers, scanners or independent readers
  • No clinical-utility or patient-outcome analysis

Primary source · DOI

Qiao Z, Zhao X, Wang G, et al. PET-based evaluation of short-term amyloid-β clearance and predictive factors in real-world Alzheimer's disease patients treated with lecanemab. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261493063.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed autopsy-confirmed PET-pathology study•September 23, 2026

Autopsy validation shows late-stage flortaucipir uptake differs across primary cortex

Among 155 autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer cases, flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices began at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory regions increasing earlier and faster than motor and somatosensory regions.

Key quantitative results: The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.

BiomarkersTau PETFlortaucipir tau PETBraak neurofibrillary tangle stageBiological staging

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117530; PMID:42830961; PMCID:PMC13634365

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Primary isocortex is usually emphasized as the terminal Braak stage, but uptake was not uniform. Visual and auditory cortex showed earlier and steeper flortaucipir increases than motor and somatosensory cortex, and age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake. The result refines late-stage spatial interpretation without validating a new treatment-selection threshold.

Study design

Researchers measured flortaucipir uptake in primary visual, auditory, motor and somatosensory isocortices in 155 participants with autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer disease, then related regional uptake to neuropathologic Braak stage and clinical or genetic covariates.

Key quantitative results

  • The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.
  • Flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices became apparent beginning at Braak stage V.
  • Visual and auditory isocortices showed greater and faster uptake increases than somatosensory and motor cortex.
  • Age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake; primary-isocortex patterns resembled lateral temporal cortex more than entorhinal cortex.

What changed

The pathology-anchored analysis shows that primary cortical regions do not behave as one homogeneous late-stage tau-PET compartment and that visual/auditory regions may signal advanced spread earlier than traditionally emphasized.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence because diagnosis and Braak stage were autopsy confirmed and the cohort was sizeable for pathology studies. The analysis remains cross-sectional and tracer-specific, and clinical utility was not tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Regional late-stage flortaucipir interpretation may need to distinguish visual and auditory cortex from motor and somatosensory cortex. The findings do not create a new authorized stage, threshold or treatment-eligibility rule.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to tau-PET visual and quantitative staging, spatial reporting, pathology concordance and discussions of how late-stage regional uptake should be interpreted.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study links regional flortaucipir uptake to neuropathologically confirmed Braak stage. It supports regional interpretation for this tracer but does not establish equivalence with other tau tracers, visual-staging schemes or quantitative pipelines.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new availability or coverage change. The study may inform specialist interpretation but does not expand access to tau PET.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does uptake in primary cortex define a new clinical stage?
No. The study refines regional relationships with neuropathologic Braak stage but does not validate a new clinical staging system.
Can the pattern be generalized to every tau tracer?
No. The evidence is specific to flortaucipir and requires tracer-specific replication.
Was treatment eligibility or response tested?
No. This was a PET-pathology interpretation study.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly published item
  • Cross-sectional analysis
  • Tracer-specific findings
  • Potential interval between PET and autopsy
  • No prospective visual-reading or treatment-decision utility test
